title: Redwood POC Weekly Sync - Benchmark Review vs Baseline Provider
summary: Weekly POC sync to review Redwood benchmark results vs the customer's current baseline provider (CloudX). We covered latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput (tokens/sec & rps), tuning knobs (KV cache, batching, quantization), and a few environment mismatches. Agreed on next runs to capture 99th percentile with prefix cache enabled and to share updated benchmark spreadsheet and cost math.
topics: KV cache and batching configuration differences
Next steps: instrumentation and benchmark reruns
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining 
 we'll try to keep to 45 minutes. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Maya: Maya here, CTO.
[00:10] Luis: Luis, ML eng.
[00:12] Samir: Samir, infra.
[00:15] Jordan: Great. Priya from Redwood is here, SE. Priya: hi all.
[00:20] Priya: I'll share the slides and the spreadsheet after, but quick recap 
 this week we focused on two workloads: convo generation for patient notes (long context ~1.2k tokens) and embedding/rerank micro-bench for search. Baseline is CloudX on a vGPU C4 equivalent.
[00:40] Luis: Quick note 
 thanks, we looked at the sheet, some of the columns looked like they were off? p99 numbers seemed lower in your sheet than our internal runs.
[00:48] Jordan: yes, good catch; part of the mismatch was sampling windows and whether KV cache was on. Priya: we had KV caching disabled in the first run to match baseline config (they didn't have prefix cache enabled). But that penalizes long conversations.
[01:05] Maya: can you remind me which model variant you used? Our baseline used the XLM-13B-fp16 from CloudX.
[01:12] Priya: for parity we used Redwood's curated 13B fp16 variant, and a quantized 13B int8 run for the high-throughput test. There was also a Redwood-dedicate style instance for the dedicated capacity runs, though the notation in the sheet says "Redwood Dedicate" which is a bit messy in transcription.
[01:30] Luis: ok. Let's go to latency numbers — you have p50/p95/p99 across both providers?
[01:38] Priya: yes I'll read them out. For convo generation (1.2k tokens) baseline CloudX p50 320ms, p95 980ms, p99 1.45s. Redwood p50 290ms, p95 720ms, p99 1.1s. These are with Redwood batching at 20ms and KV cache off.
[02:00] Samir: those p99 improvements look good. How repeatable are they? I guess p99 is sensitive to tail network jitter.
[02:08] Priya: agreed; we ran 10k requests for each config, across 3 hours, and the standard deviation on p99 was ~8-12% depending on load. We also saw that enabling prefix KV cache reduces p95/p99 a lot for long session reuse cases — roughly 25-40% improvement on tail.
[02:30] Maya: can you explain the KV cache difference again? Baseline provider said they cache at runtime but not across requests?
[02:36] Jordan: baseline CloudX had per-request KV but no cross-request prefix cache persisted in their setup. Redwood's runtime supports KV cache persistence per session and automatic prefix eviction; that was off in the parity run but we tested it on the follow-up.
[02:50] Priya: with KV cache on, Redwood convo generation p50 270ms, p95 540ms, p99 820ms. So p99 moved from 1.1s to 0.82s in our internal runs.
[03:02] Luis: interesting. What about throughput? requests per second and tokens/sec?
[03:06] Priya: throughput for the embedding micro-bench (short requests) — baseline CloudX sustained 240 rps, tokens/sec ~12k. Redwood int8 quantized run sustained 410 rps, tokens/sec ~20k on the same instance class. For generation long seqs the baseline had better single-request latency under low load but Redwood scales better under concurrency because of continuous batching and better kernel selection.
[03:30] Samir: is the hardware the same? Are we comparing apples to apples?
[03:34] Priya: mostly — we matched GPU class but there are differences in NIC config and instance CPU. We documented CPU utilization; in some baseline runs their CPU was pegged which inflated tail latency. We noted that in the sheet.
[03:48] Maya: do you have the raw logs? We want to validate the p99 claims.
[03:52] Jordan: yes we'll share the raw aggregated histograms and the benchmark spreadsheet. We can't share full host logs for hosted runs but we can provide aggregated percentiles and exportable histograms.
[04:02] Luis: what's the cost delta? If Redwood is faster but more expensive, we need the math.
[04:06] Priya: short answer: with quantization and batching, Redwood's per-token cost for the embedding workload was ~0.018 USD per 1k tokens equivalent, baseline was 0.027 USD; so about 30% lower. For convo gen if you need dedicated capacity Redwood's reserved SKU pricing is in the sheet. The caveat is queuing and batch sizing tradeoffs for single-user low-latency cases.
[04:30] Samir: can you expand on batch sizing tradeoffs?
[04:32] Priya: sure — we tuned continuous batching window between 10-40ms. For latency-sensitive single requests you reduce the window to 10ms which reduces batching efficiency and increases cost. For high concurrency you can raise to 30-40ms and get better throughput and lower unit cost but slightly higher p50.
[04:50] Maya: we care about tail behavior more than average. The p99 is the one that impacts user experience.
[04:55] Priya: totally — which is why the KV cache and CPU headroom matter. Also auto-fallback to a smaller model variant helps preserve latency at cost of a small degradation in quality. We showed A/B suggestions in the doc.
[05:08] Luis: you mentioned quantization — any regression in quality? Our evaluation set is sensitive to hallucinations.
[05:14] Priya: we ran the quality evals on our standard prompt set — int8 quant gave <1% delta on Rouge/semantic similarity for most prompts, but a small increase in tokenization variance for some tricky prompts. We'll mark those prompts in the quality sheet.
[05:28] Jordan: also worth noting throughput numbers for burst workloads — Redwood's smart routing can spin up burst capacity on dedicated pools, CloudX had fixed burst behavior in their environment which caused queueing in our tests.
[05:42] Samir: what about security/compliance — we have to run this in VPC for PHI. Baseline vendor had VPC peering. Can Redwood replicate?
[05:50] Jordan: yes Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem. For the POC we ran in our dedicated test VPC with customer-managed KMS example. We have SOC2 + in-progress ISO notes in the security doc. We'll share the SOC2 report and the network diagram.
[06:06] Maya: that's good. OK can we move to discrepancies — Luis you flagged two rows with odd p99 in the sheet?
[06:12] Luis: yeah row 48 and 51 — the comment says "burst run" but it looks like a different config (batching window was 100ms?). That inflated p50 but also dropped tokens/sec.
[06:22] Priya: that was an accidental config — thanks for catching. We'll re-run with the corrected batching window.
[06:27] Jordan: next I want to cover mini-run results we did after parity: we enabled prefix cache, set batching window to 20ms, and ran a 1 hour 5k req test. The p99 improved 28% vs the parity run and tokens/sec improved 18% vs baseline.
[06:45] Maya: sounds promising. Any unexpected failure modes?
[06:47] Priya: one instance of OOM in the quantized path during the first warmup due to a mis-compiled kernel in our older runtime; patched in the afternoon and re-run. We logged that as a bug and fixed it — notes in the sheet.
[07:02] Luis: can you tag which runs used the patched runtime? We need to be sure the numbers reflect the fixed one.
[07:07] Priya: yes — runs with suffix _r2 used the patched runtime. We'll filter in the sheet.
[07:12] Samir: on the infra side, how much ops work to transition? We have terraform templates?
[07:16] Jordan: we have a Terraform module plus a quickstart that does VPC peering, IAM roles, and KMS integration. For Dedicated we can do a managed setup or an infra-as-code approach; both options are documented.
[07:28] Maya: timeline — if we like the numbers, we want a 4-week pilot in prod to evaluate end-to-end. Is that realistic?
[07:34] Jordan: yes typical pilot is 3-6 weeks. For a production pilot we recommend starting with a small percentage of traffic and a canary route for 2 weeks then scale.
[07:42] Luis: what instrumentation should we add? We want consistent histograms, structured traces, and token-level cost.
[07:48] Priya: we'll add our trace hooks and a lightweight SDK that emits p50/p95/p99 histograms and token counts. We can also push traces to your Jaeger or DataDog.
[07:58] Maya: fine. Should we have Redwood run another full benchmark with KV cache ON and patched runtime and long-run 10k req?
[08:04] Priya: yes we'll run that and include two runs: one with prefix KV enabled and one with it disabled; both with patched runtime and consistent batch window.
[08:12] Jordan: ok let's recap next steps and owners.
[08:16] Jordan: Next steps: share updated benchmark spreadsheet and histograms (Jordan), schedule a 4-week pilot proposal and pricing (Jordan), Priya to run the new parity runs with KV on and patched runtime and upload results by Monday, and team to review security docs (Maya).
[08:30] Samir: can you also include cost math for steady-state and burst scenarios?
[08:34] Priya: yes will include run-level cost and reserved vs on-demand comparisons.
[08:38] Maya: fine. Any other questions?
[08:40] Luis: one quick one — can we get raw traces for one failing p99 sample? to dig deeper.
[08:44] Priya: we can provide sanitized traces and waterfall breakdowns.
[08:48] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll share the artifacts.
[08:50] Maya: thanks. bye.
[08:52] [call ends]
